parts.problem_md:
The root-mean-square input potential difference to the full-wave rectifier is 14.1 V.

The frequency of the input potential difference is 40 Hz.

On Fig. 1.2, draw a graph of the potential difference across the load resistor for 2.5 periods, choosing a sensible scale for the y axis.

parts.solution_md:
To draw 2.5 periods of the rectified wave:

List the known quantities:

- Root-mean-square voltage, *V*<sub>*rms*</sub>  = 14.1 V
- Frequency, *f*  = 40 Hz

Determine the period:

- $T=\frac{1}{f}=\frac{1}{40}=25\mathrm{ms}$

Determine the peak voltage, *V*<sub>0</sub> :

- $V_{rms}=\frac{V_{0}}{\sqrt{2}}$
- $V_{0}=14.1\times\sqrt{2}=19.9V$

A graph gaining 3 marks looks like:

![rectifier-graph-ma](assets/004-rectifier-graph-ma.png)

- Peaks reach 19.9 V (± one small square) **AND **are more than half the height of the graph paper; **[1 mark]**
- Correct shape for a full-wave rectified alternating potential difference; **[1 mark]**
- Five peaks filling the x axis **AND** labelled as being 12.5 ms across each; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *For 2.5 periods to fill the graph paper, there are 10 squares so each period must take up 4 squares horizontally, with the last 0.5 of a period taking 2 squares.*

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

The root-mean-square input potential difference to the full-wave rectifier is 14.1 V. The frequency of the input potential difference is 40 Hz. On Fig. 1.2, draw a graph of the potential difference across the load resistor for 2.5 periods, choosing a sensible scale for the y axis.

The circuit in Fig. 1.1 is then modified by two students. One student adds a single capacitor, as shown in Fig. 1.3. The other adds two capacitors in series, as shown in Fig. 1.4.

![21-2-q1c-2-h-sq-cie-ial-physics](assets/005-21-2-q1c-2-h-sq-cie-ial-physics.png)

** **

**Fig. 1.3**

![21-2-q1c-h-sq-cie-ial-physics](assets/006-21-2-q1c-h-sq-cie-ial-physics.png)

**Fig. 1.4**

Compare the effects of each modification on the graph you drew on Fig. 1.2, when both circuits are completed to form full-wave rectifiers. Explain any differences.
parts.solution_md:
Comparing the effects of each capacitor configuration on the output signal:

- The single capacitor <u>smooths</u> the peaks in the output voltage; **[1 mark]**
- The two capacitors <u>smooth</u> the peaks <u>less than</u> the single capacitor; **[1 mark]**
- (Therefore) there are larger fluctuations / ripples in the output voltage with the two capacitors; **[1 mark]**

Explain the difference:

- Because capacitors in series have a <u>lower capacitance</u>; **[1 mark]**
- (Therefore) the time constant is smaller; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

> *Recall that capacitors in series have a combined capacitance according to the following equation:*

$\frac{1}{C_{tot}}=\frac{1}{C_{1}}+\frac{1}{C_{2}}$

> *This means total capacitance is less than the individual capacitance of either capacitor, i.e. adding capacitors in series reduces total capacitance. This means the time constant is smaller, so the capacitor system discharges faster and the output voltage dips more in between input peaks. *

parts.problem_md:
The graph in Fig. 1.4 shows the output of an ac generator after undergoing half-wave rectification.

![11-2-sq-5d-question_hl-sq-medium](assets/015-11-2-sq-5d-question-hl-sq-medium.png)

**Fig. 1.4.**

The load resistor has a resistance of 3.6 kΩ. Capacitors of capacitance 360 nF and 60 µF are available.

Determine which of the capacitors would be the most appropriate to smooth the output in Fig. 1.4.
parts.solution_md:
Determine the correct capacitor to use for smoothing the output:

List the known quantities:

- Resistance, *R* = 3.6 k Ω = 3600 Ω
- Time interval between adjacent peaks, *t* = 40 ms = 40 × 10<sup>−3</sup> s (from the graph)
- Capacitor 1, *C*<sub>*1*</sub> = 360 nF = 360 × 10<sup>−9</sup> F
- Capacitor 2, *C*<sub>*2*</sub> = 60 µF = 60 × 10<sup>−6</sup> F

Calculate the time constants for both capacitors:

- Time constant:  $T=RC$
- Capacitor 1:  $T_{1}=3600\times(360\times10^{-9})=1.3\times10^{-3}s$
- Capacitor 2:  $T_{2}=3600\times(60\times10^{-6})=0.216s$

Compare the time constants of the capacitors with the time between peaks:

- The time constant of capacitor 1, *T*<sub>*1*</sub> = 1.3 × 10<sup>−3</sup> s, is <u>less than</u> the time interval, *t* = 40 × 10<sup>−3</sup> s; **[1 mark]**
- So, the output will <u>not</u> be smoothed significantly:

![11-2-sq-5d-mark-scheme-2_hl-sq-medium](assets/016-11-2-sq-5d-mark-scheme-2-hl-sq-medium.png)

- The time constant of capacitor 2, *T*<sub>*2*</sub> = 0.216 s, is much <u>greater than</u> the time interval, *t* = 40 × 10<sup>−3</sup> s; **[1 mark]**
- So, the output will be smoothed significantly:

![11-2-sq-5d-mark-scheme-1_hl-sq-medium](assets/017-11-2-sq-5d-mark-scheme-1-hl-sq-medium.png)

State the most appropriate capacitor to smooth the output correctly:

- The <u>60 µF</u> capacitor; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

(i) On Fig. 5.1, draw a line to show *V*<sub>OUT</sub> between times *t* = 1.0 ms and *t* = 5.0 ms.

parts.solution_md:
(i) A graph that would score 3 marks:

![file-000-48](assets/021-file-000-48.png)

- The minimum potential difference is 8.0 − 2.0 = 6.0 V; **[1 mark]**
- Straight line drawn from peak $V_{0}$ at t = 1.0 ms to minimum (non-zero) value where it meets the printed line after 4.0 ms; **[1 mark]**
- The printed curve is followed to its peak at 5.0 ms; **[1 mark]**

(ii) Determine the time, in s, for which the capacitor is discharging between times *t* = 1.0 ms and *t* = 5.0 ms:

![file-000-49](assets/022-file-000-49.png)

- From the graph:

  - The capacitor begins discharging at *t *= 1.0 ms
  - The capacitor stops discharging at *t *= 4.5 ms

- Δ*t *= 4.5 − 1.0 = 3.5 ms = 3.5 × 10<sup>−3</sup> s **[1 mark]**

(iii) Use your answers in **(b)(i)** and **(b)(ii)** to calculate the resistance *R:*

List the known quantities:

- Output voltage, $V$ = 6.0 V
- Peak voltage, $V_{0}$ = 8.0 V
- Time to discharge, $t$ = 3.5 × 10<sup>−3</sup> s
- Capacitance of the capacitor, $C$ = 85 μF = 85 × 10<sup>−6</sup> F

Use the capacitor discharge equation in terms of voltage:

- $V=V_{0}e^{-\frac{t}{RC}}$ **[1 mark]**
- $\frac{V}{V_{0}}=e^{-\frac{t}{RC}}$
- $\ln ( \frac{V}{V} _{0} ) = - \frac{t}{R C}$
- `R = (- t)/(C ln ( V / V _ 0 ))`

Substitute the known quantities into the equation:

- $R = \frac{- ( 3.5 \times 10^{- 3} )}{( 85 \times 10^{- 6} ) \ln ( \frac{6}{8} )}$ **[1 mark]**
- `R = 143 capital omega = 140 capital omega ( 2 s. f. )` **[1 mark]**

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Fig. 1.1 shows four diodes and a load resistor of resistance, 2.4 kΩ, connected in a circuit that is used to produce rectification of an alternating voltage. Fig. 1.1

A sinusoidal alternating voltage V_IN is applied across the input terminals X and Y. The variation of time t of V_IN is given by the equation V_IN = 3.0 sin(20πt) where V_IN is in volts and t is in seconds. The magnitude of the output voltage V_OUT varies with t as shown in Fig. 1.2. Max V_OUT = 3.0 V; Angular frequency ω = 20π; Time period T = 2π/ω = 0.1 s. The t scale is labelled 0.025, 0.05, 0.075, 0.1, 0.125 and 0.15 on the tick marks and V_OUT scale labelled 2 and 4 on the tick marks.

The output voltage in **(b) **is smoothed by adding a capacitor to the circuit in Fig. 1.1.

The difference between the maximum and minimum values of the smoothed output voltage is 15% of the peak voltage.

(i) On Fig. 1.1, draw the circuit symbol for a capacitor showing the capacitor correctly connected into the circuit.

[1]

(ii) On Fig. 1.2, sketch the variation with *t *of the smoothed output voltage.

[2]
parts.solution_md:
(i) A capacitor correctly drawn onto the circuit is as follows:

![b1735d23-520a-4347-86ab-9c29d2c14dd3](assets/042-b1735d23-520a-4347-86ab-9c29d2c14dd3.jpeg)

- Correct symbol used for capacitor, and the capacitor is connected in parallel with the 2.4 kΩ resistor; **[1 mark]**

(ii) The graph of the smooth output voltage that should score 2 marks would look like this:

Calculate 15% of the peak voltage:

- 3 × 0.15 = 0.45
- So, the peak voltage falls by 0.45 V to 2.55 V

![Smoothing Capacitor Q1c MA](assets/043-smoothing-capacitor-q1c-ma.png)

- Straight line sections (between the peak voltage and reduced voltage) have a negative gradient **AND **are drawn as shown; **[1 mark]**
- The lines between adjacent curves show a drop in p.d. of 0.45 V / just over 2 small squares;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**
